title: The Main Thread & Task Model
objectives: Explain how the browser schedules tasks and what makes a task long
Estimate blocking time from task durations using the 50 ms threshold
Break up long work with chunking so input stays responsive
Read a network waterfall to find what actually delayed the page
body:
Inside each browser tab there is one main thread that runs your JavaScript, style recalculation, layout, paint bookkeeping and input handling — in most cases all of it, one task at a time. The browser pulls tasks off a queue and runs each to completion. When one task hogs the thread, everything else waits: clicks, keypresses, rendering.

## The problem
Your dashboard recalculates a large table when the user clicks Refresh. On fast machines it feels fine; on a mid-range phone the tab freezes for a second and taps land late. The team wants to know how bad it is in numbers, not vibes.

## Constraints
- A task that runs longer than **50 ms** is a *long task*; everything queued behind it is delayed.
- For responsiveness, what matters is not total time but the largest slice the user must wait for.
- INP (Interaction to Next Paint) is dominated by input delay — the time a tap waits for the current task to finish.
- You cannot abort a running task; the only way out is to never start one that long.

## Options
Given 200 ms of work, you can run it as one task, or yield between chunks:

```js
// One 200 ms task: input waits up to 200 ms → jank
processAll(rows)

// Chunked: ~6 tasks of ~33 ms; the queue drains between chunks
async function processAll(rows) {
  for (let i = 0; i < rows.length; i++) {
    processRow(rows[i])
    if (i % 50 === 49) await nextTick() // setTimeout(0) or scheduler.yield()
  }
}
function nextTick() {
  return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 0))
}
```

Chunking adds a little total time (the loop overhead, plus queued rendering in between) but caps the worst-case wait. `scheduler.yield()` is the purpose-built API where available; `setTimeout(0)` is the portable fallback. A Web Worker is the third option when the work does not touch the DOM.

## Tradeoffs
Chunking trades peak latency for total throughput: the same work takes slightly longer wall-clock time but the UI stays alive. Workers remove the work from the main thread entirely, at the cost of structured-clone message passing and no DOM access. Doing nothing is cheapest to write and most expensive for users.

## Decision
If a task is measured above 50 ms on representative hardware and runs during interaction, split it. Prefer `scheduler.yield()` inside the loop, fall back to `setTimeout`, and move pure computation (parsing, sorting, crypto) to a Worker when it grows beyond tens of milliseconds.

## Measure it
Record the interaction in the Performance panel and read the main thread track: each block is a task, and warnings flag the ones over 50 ms. For field data, observe `PerformanceObserver` with `type: "longtask"`, and track INP via the web-vitals library — before and after every change.

## Best practices
- Treat 50 ms as the ceiling for any task that can run during an interaction.
- Yield inside long loops every few milliseconds of work, not just once.
- Move pure computation off the main thread with Workers when it dominates.
- Read network waterfalls bottom-up: the first blocked request usually explains the delay.
- Capture a baseline task trace before refactoring, and compare after.

## Common mistakes
- Measuring average task time and missing the single 400 ms outlier that users actually feel.
- Assuming `await` of a plain function yields to the browser — only real timers, scheduler APIs or microtask boundaries let pending tasks in.
- Moving DOM work into a Worker and discovering Workers cannot touch the DOM.
- Blaming the network for slow interactions when the waterfall shows the page idle but the main thread pegged.
- Shipping the fix without re-recording, so the long task quietly survives in another code path.

exercise.prompt: Given a list of task durations in milliseconds, compute for each task whether it is a long task (over 50 ms) and how many milliseconds of it are blocking (the part above 50). Render a verdict row per task plus a total blocking time line. The blocking calculation is missing — implement it.
hints: A task of 210 ms blocks for 160 ms: everything above 50 counts.
Math.max(0, ms - 50) expresses the rule in one line.
Keep verdict() separate from blocking() so the label and the number stay independent.

questions.prompt: What is the duration threshold above which a task is considered a long task?
questions.explanation: The long task API and the interaction-latency guidance both use 50 ms as the point where a task starts to meaningfully delay input and rendering.

questions.prompt: Why does splitting a 200 ms task into ten 20 ms chunks improve responsiveness?
options: It reduces the total CPU time the work needs
It lets queued input handling and rendering run between chunks
It moves the work onto the GPU automatically
It disables the browser task queue while the chunks run
questions.explanation: Chunking does not shrink the work; it creates gaps where the browser can process pending input and paint, which is exactly what INP measures.
